# Production Function Parameters and Productivity {#sec-pf}

<!-- Ported 2026-09-24 (see Thesis/REUSE-LOG.md). Visible prose is copied from

and Paper/sections/250-pf.qmd (discussion of the elasticities), with notation translated: the approved

Materials overreporting biases the production-function and productivity estimates of proxy-variable methods that rely on a flexible input [@Levinsohn2003; @Doraszelski2013; @Ackerberg2015; @Gandhi2020]. These methods typically use materials as the flexible input. For example, the output elasticity of materials can be recovered from the materials log share of output [@Gandhi2020]. Since reported materials are inflated, the estimate of the elasticity is too large. This bias then permeates the rest of the production-function parameters and productivity.

In [this chapter]{.content-hidden when-meta="jmp"}[this section]{.content-visible when-meta="jmp"}, I show how to recover the remaining parameters of the production function, the elasticities of capital and labour, and productivity net of overreporting.

Failing to correct for overreporting leads to a larger output elasticity of materials and more dispersed and less persistent productivity. Uncorrected estimates overstate the ratio of the 90th to the 10th percentile of productivity by 66 percent and understate the half-life of productivity shocks by 63 percent, in the median of the five industries.

## Identification {#sec-pf-identification}

In the literature, it is not uncommon to assume that productivity follows a Markov process. That is,

$$
    \omega_{it}=g(\omega_{it-1})+\eta_{it}
$$ {#eq-prod-markov}

Let $\ln X_{it}=x_{it}$. With @eq-ob-ev, I can form the following observed variable,

$$
\begin{aligned}
    \mathcal W_{it} & \equiv y_{it} - \beta (m^*_{it}-\mathcal{V}_{it})\\
    & = y_{it} - \beta (m_{it}+u_{it}-u_{it}+\varepsilon_{it})\\
    & = y_{it} - \beta m_{it}-\beta\varepsilon_{it}\\
    & = \alpha_K k_{it}+\alpha_L l_{it}+\omega_{it}+(1-\beta)\varepsilon_{it}
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-big-w}

Here, intuitively, I am trading unobservables: the unobserved tax evasion for the measurement error. Also note that it is not necessary to learn tax evasion to recover productivity. This is useful if a practitioner is only interested in productivity and not in tax evasion.

By replacing $\omega_{it}$ from @eq-big-w in @eq-prod-markov, I get

$$
\begin{aligned}
    \mathcal W_{it}=(1-\beta)\varepsilon_{it}+\alpha_K k_{it}+\alpha_L l_{it}+g(\mathcal W_{it-1}-(1-\beta)\varepsilon_{it-1}-\alpha_K k_{it-1}-\alpha_L l_{it-1})+\eta_{it}
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-big-w-reg}

If $g(\xi)=\gamma_0 +\gamma_1\xi$, to learn $\alpha$ and $g$, I can use instruments $Z$ such that,

$$
\mathbb{E}[\eta_{it}+(1-\beta)\varepsilon_{it}+\gamma_1(1-\beta)\varepsilon_{it-1}|Z]=0.
$$ {#eq-eta-moments}

As the instrument, I use $\widetilde{\mathcal W}_{it-2}$, the residual defined below in @eq-w-squiggle, lagged two years. $\widetilde{\mathcal W}_{it-2}$ is correlated with past productivity but independent of the innovation and of the two measurement errors in @eq-eta-moments. @sec-app-pf-estimation provides details of the estimation.

Once the parameters of the production function are identified, I can use the following observed variable to recover $\omega_{it}$,

$$
\begin{aligned}
    \widetilde{\mathcal W}_{it} & \equiv \mathcal W_{it} - \alpha_K k_{it}-\alpha_L l_{it}\\
    & = \omega_{it}+(1-\beta)\varepsilon_{it}
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-w-squiggle}

I recover the distribution of productivity net of measurement error by deconvolving $\widetilde{\mathcal W}_{it}=\omega_{it}+(1-\beta)\varepsilon_{it}$ with the corporations' distribution of measurement error, as in @sec-deconvolution.

## Production function and productivity estimates {#sec-pf-estimates}

The estimates cover the five industries of @sec-deconvolution; @sec-app-pf-all reports all nine industries of the structural estimation.

::: {#tbl-pf-comparison}
![](/tables/ch06-pf-comparison.png)

Production function estimates by method: evasion-corrected with instrument $\tilde{\mathcal W}_{it-2}$, and uncorrected GNR and OLS. Below each corrected estimate, the 95 percent test-inversion regions (sharp and conservative). Other instruments: @tbl-pf-instruments.
:::

Because tax evasion artificially inflates the materials' cost share of revenues, lower output elasticities of materials than those of traditional methods are expected. @tbl-pf-comparison shows that correcting for tax evasion results in smaller output elasticities of materials than both OLS and GNR in all five industries.

The elasticities of capital and labour vary across industries, with some being lower than the uncorrected estimates, some higher, and others quite similar. This is expected. The direction of the bias in the elasticities of capital and labour depends on whether these inputs are complements or substitutes for materials. This relationship will vary by industry. Put differently, the cross-elasticities of materials with capital and with labour differ across industries in direction and magnitude. Since these cross-elasticities are not included in the Cobb-Douglas production function, the elasticities of capital and labour should reflect different degrees of these variations once materials are corrected for overreporting.

Correcting for overreporting also reduces dispersion in productivity. The 90th-to-10th-percentile ratio of $\exp(\omega_{it})$ is 1.70 to 2.30 with the correction, against 2.38 to 6.86 for GNR. In the median of the five industries, the uncorrected ratio is 66 percent larger (range 23 to 291 percent; @tbl-productivity-comparison).

<!-- Productivity estimates in [this chapter]{.content-hidden when-meta="jmp"}[this section]{.content-visible when-meta="jmp"} use the $\tilde{\mathcal W}_{it-2}$ estimates of @tbl-pf-comparison.  -->

::: {#tbl-productivity-comparison}
![](/tables/ch06-productivity-comparison.png)

Productivity corrected for tax evasion (deconvolved, instrument $\tilde{\mathcal W}_{it-2}$) and uncorrected (GNR), by industry.
:::

Correcting for overreporting also makes productivity more persistent. With instrument $\tilde{\mathcal W}_{it-2}$, the AR(1) coefficient of $\omega_{it}$ is 0.93 to 0.96 across the five industries, against 0.81 to 0.89 for GNR. The half-life of a productivity shock, $\ln 0.5/\ln\hat\gamma_1$, is therefore 9 to 15 years with the correction and 3 to 6 years without it. In the median of the five industries, the uncorrected half-life is 63 percent shorter (range 37 to 67 percent; @tbl-productivity-comparison).

Three caveats apply to @tbl-productivity-comparison. First, the P-spline penalty smooths the deconvolved density, which can understate its dispersion, whereas the firm-level GNR estimates of $\omega_{it}$ carry estimation noise, which can overstate it. Second, @Gandhi2020 define productivity in levels as $\exp(\omega_{it}+\varepsilon_{it})$, with $\varepsilon_{it}$ an ex-post output shock. Here, $\varepsilon_{it}$ is measurement error in output, and productivity is $\exp(\omega_{it})$. The GNR estimates in @tbl-productivity-comparison use the same convention: both compare $\omega_{it}$ with $\omega_{it}$, and their published productivity ratios are not directly comparable with these. Third, the two persistence estimates come from different estimators: the corrected $\hat\gamma_1$ is an instrumental-variables estimate within the production-function step, whereas the GNR $\hat\gamma_1$ is a least-squares regression of firm-level $\omega_{it}$ on its lag, which estimation noise in $\omega_{it}$ biases towards zero. Part of the gap in persistence, and so in half-lives, may reflect this difference rather than overreporting.
